title: AI and the Faustian Bargain
passage:
What is the problem to which this technology is the solution?

Whose problem is it?

What new problems will be created by solving the old one?

Which people and institutions will be most harmed?

What changes in language are being forced by the new technology?

What shifts in economic and political power might result?

What alternate uses might be made of the technology?
source: Neil Postman, from The Surrender of Culture to Technology (1997 lecture), building on his book Technopoly (1992).
reflection:
Postman wasn't talking about AI — he was talking about television, computers, the internet, the wave of technologies that arrived promising to make life easier and quietly rearranged everything underneath us. Postman frames every technological adoption as a Faustian bargain, after the legend of the scholar who sells his soul for knowledge and power — he gets exactly what he asked for. That is the trap: the bargain is never advertised as a bargain. It is advertised as a gift.

Before you introduce AI into your product, your process, or your team's daily workflow, run the questions. Not as a formality. As the actual gate. The bargain will get made either way. The only choice you have is whether you read the fine print at the bottom of the contract first.

title: Sand in the Sandwich
passage:
Every efficiency gain from AI comes as a trade — sand in the sandwich. We can generate subtitles for almost any video with near-zero effort; knowledge gets more accessible, more democratized. But we accept errors in exchange. The question that matters is not whether errors will appear. They will. The question is how much error we are willing to swallow for a cheaper, faster process.

And once output looks plausible, review doesn't save us. The brain switches off its own error detection — what Høst calls output blindness. Humans are far better at constructing something correct than at verifying something already built. Verification is passive; construction keeps the mind engaged. So the workflow most teams lean on — AI generates, human checks — is broken by design. The check happens exactly when the checker is least equipped to do it.
source: Einar W. Høst, talk on AI narratives and harms — Vimeo / YouTube.
reflection:
This talk has stayed with me. It made me think hard about how I use AI — privately, and professionally during product development. Not the pitch version. The real one, powers and harms both.

Subtitles are, relatively, low stakes. A wrong word is an annoyance. But what does the same trade-off mean for software as a medical device? How much sand are we willing to accept when the text in question is a risk assessment, a clinical claim, a piece of documentation someone downstream will trust without re-checking? And if the answer is none, or close to none, how do we actually keep the sand out, rather than just hoping we notice it once it's already in the sandwich?

Which is where output blindness bites hardest. If review is not the safety net we assumed it was, what does keeping the sand out actually look like in a SaMD context?

title: You Cannot Step Into the Same River Twice
passage: You cannot step into the same river twice, because other waters are always flowing toward you. The river keeps its name. The water never repeats.
source: Heraclitus, c. 500 BCE — preserved as a fragment through Plato's Cratylus. I was reminded of it by DHH (David Heinemeier Hansson), on his appearance on the Lex Fridman Podcast.
reflection: I keep running into this one in places that have nothing to do with philosophy. Every year I go back to my country of origin for the holidays. My parents, relatives, old friends still carry an image of who I was when I left. But that person does not exist anymore. Years abroad, different work, different daily pressures, they all reshaped me into someone they are not fully familiar with. And it runs both ways. They have changed too, in ways I only half see because I am not there for the slow accumulation of it. We meet expecting the old river. We get new water. Same thing watching my daughters grow. One year they are children. A few years later they are teenagers with their own opinions, their own friction points, their own version of the world. I cannot parent the teenager the way I parented the child, even though she carries the same name and the same photographs from before. Software has its own version of this. Customer requirements are never the fixed thing a contract or a spec implies. What a product needed to do a month ago is not what it needs to do now. Cybersecurity is a clean example. Requirements that barely existed a few months back now show up mid-sprint, forcing teams to rework priorities around demands that were not there when the roadmap was first drawn. Nobody planned poorly. The regulatory water just kept moving. The lesson is not to plan harder so the river holds still. It won't. Since requirements change constantly, the only sane response is to accept change itself as the one constant and build the capacity to adjust to it as it comes, rather than treating the original plan as sacred. This is exactly what the Agile Manifesto and its authors have been advocating since 2001: "responding to change over following a plan." Two decades on, teams still relearn it the hard way, project by project, because the instinct to defend the original spec is stronger than the evidence that the water has already moved. The mistake, in families and in product development, is treating the name as if it guarantees the substance. It does not. The river is still called a river. The product is still called the same product. But what is actually flowing through it changes constantly, and pretending otherwise is how you end up planning for a version of the world that already left.

title: Dissatisfaction Is an Acquired Taste
passage:
Hedonic adaptation — a fancy term that simply means what once felt extraordinary becomes ordinary over time. Last year’s raise is now the paycheck you expect every two weeks. And yesterday’s upgrade is now today’s obsolescence.

The thing we obtain isn’t the flashy car or the giant house or the impressive job title. What we really acquire is a taste for those things — a synthetic thirst that now needs repeated quenching. So in a real way, dissatisfaction is an acquired taste.

This is why the path of improvement eventually leads to deficiency. The moment we decide water must taste better, we have declared that water itself is insufficient.
source: The Minimalists (Joshua Fields Millburn & Ryan Nicodemus). See also the hedonic treadmill.
reflection: What stuck with me is the reversal. I always thought I was chasing the thing — the camera, the raise, the better apartment. But what I really pick up is the wanting. The thing wears off fast; the taste for it stays. That’s the trap of an inflated lifestyle: earn a bit more and the new amount just becomes normal, so the raise that made me happy in month one is simply the salary I expect by month three. So the real question about the mirrorless camera isn’t can I afford it, or even would it take better photos. It’s: am I buying a tool, or am I buying a new want that I’ll have to feed again in a couple of months? If the happiness only lasts a few weeks, I’m not really buying an object — I’m signing up for the next craving. “The moment we decide water must taste better, we have declared that water itself is insufficient.” The point isn’t to give everything up. It’s to learn that the water is already enough.

title: The Optimist and the Pessimist
passage: The optimist proclaims that we live in the best of all possible worlds; and the pessimist fears this is true.
source: James Branch Cabell, The Silver Stallion: A Comedy of Redemption (1926) — Book Four, ch. XXVI, “The Realist in Defeat,” spoken by the character Coth. Again by way of Έρωτας και άλλες πολεμικές τέχνες.
reflection: The optimist and the pessimist say the same thing — this is the best of all possible worlds — but one proclaims it and the other fears it is true. They don’t disagree about the world; they just feel differently about it. (The line is often credited to Oppenheimer, who quoted a looser version. The original is Cabell’s, twenty years earlier.)

title: The Ninety-Ninth Night
passage: A mandarin fell in love with a courtesan. She told him she would be his if he waited for her, sitting on a stool in her garden, for one hundred nights in a row. He agreed, and night after night he sat beneath her window, patient and unmoving. On the ninety-ninth night, with only one night left, he suddenly rose, tucked his stool under his arm, and walked away.
source: Retold by Roland Barthes in A Lover’s Discourse: Fragments (1977), in the fragment “Waiting.” I first met it in Έρωτας και άλλες πολεμικές τέχνες.
reflection: That is the whole story. No reason is given for why he leaves — and the silence is the point. It is usually read as a meditation on desire and waiting. One reading says his desire died precisely because it was about to be satisfied: the anticipation was the love, and possession would only have ended it. Another reads pride into it — a man who will not be tested to the very last inch, and who reclaims himself by refusing the final step. A third finds simple exhaustion: the limit of any patience, which can turn, without warning, into refusal. Barthes uses it to show how the lover’s waiting is “unbearable” — how devotion and abandonment sit closer together than we like to think. What I find striking is where the story comes from. Barthes borrowed it from the Japanese legend of the poet Ono no Komachi and Captain Fukakusa no Shōshō — “The Hundred Nights.” In the original, the suitor does not walk away on the last night. He dies on it. Barthes’ quiet edit — turning a death into a decision — is the whole difference between tragedy and freedom. The captain is defeated by the hundredth night; the mandarin defeats it.
